en: The Sūtra on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under the Pippala Tree, also known as the Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination Heard in the City of Śrāvastī,
translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu Kingdom.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
On that occasion, the Buddha addressed [the monks]:
“Bhikkhu! The bhikkhu should then reply:
“Yes, Venerable Sir.”
The bhikṣus listened to the Buddha.
The Buddha then spoke, saying: "O bhikṣus!"
When I was originally a bodhisattva who had not yet attained the Buddha-way, I reflected thus: "Alas!
This world is extremely agonizing, characterized by birth, old age, and death; one goes forth only to undergo suffering."
"When will one obtain liberation from old age and death?
"O bhikṣus! They then reflected within themselves and attained this thought:"
"For what reason is there old age and death?
By what causes and conditions, furthermore, does old age and death come to be?
"O Bhikṣus! [Thus he spoke.]
He then reflected on the origin and attained realization according to his intention:
"Because of birth there is old age and death; furthermore, with birth as a condition, there is old age and death. "Monks! [he said].
He then reflected:
"For what purpose does birth exist?
And by what causes and conditions does one take birth again?"
"O Bhikṣu! He then reflected according to his original mindfulness and attained this realization:
'Because of existence there is birth; furthermore, because of the conditions of existence, there is again birth.'"
"Monks! He then reflects and gives rise to this thought:
'For what reason does existence come to be?'"
"By what causes and conditions does it exist again? Monks,
he then reflected according to his original mindfulness, and this thought arose in him:
"Because of grasping there is becoming; furthermore, with grasping as a condition, there is becoming. "Monks!
One then reflects:"
"For what reason does existence arise? And by what causes and conditions does one further undergo existence?
"Monks! [the Buddha said.]
Then, following his original reflection, he attained this realization:
"It is for the sake of craving that one experiences [feeling], and through the causal condition of craving, one further experiences [feeling]. "O Bhikṣus!"
He then reflected:
"For what reason does craving exist?
And by what causes and conditions does craving arise?"
"Monks! He then contemplated according to his original reflections and attained this essential point:
'Because of pleasant feeling there is craving; furthermore, because of the causal conditions of pleasant feeling, there is craving.'"
"Monks! He then reflects and considers:
'By what means do suffering and pleasure exist?'"
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do painful and pleasant feelings arise? Monks,
he then reflected according to his original mindfulness and attained this realization:
"Furthermore, there is feeling and pleasure arising from contact, and feeling and pleasure arise again with contact as their condition.
"Monks! He then reflects and contemplates thus:"
“Why is there further becoming?
And by what causes and conditions does further becoming arise?
“Monks! [the Buddha said.]
Then, reflecting upon the original teaching and contemplating it, this thought arose in accordance with his mind:
"Because of the six sense bases there is contact; furthermore, with the six sense bases as condition, there is contact. "Monks!"
He then reflected:
"For what reason do the six sense bases exist?
By what causes and conditions, moreover, do the six sense bases come to be?"
"Monks! He then reflected according to his original mindfulness and attained this realization:
'Because of name-and-form there are the six sense bases; furthermore, because of name-and-form as a condition, there are the six sense bases.'"
"Monks! He then reflects and contemplates:
'For what reason do names and forms exist?'"
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do names and forms arise? Monks,
he then reflected according to his original mindfulness and attained this realization:
"Because of consciousness, there is the existence of name-and-form; furthermore, with consciousness as a condition, there is again name-and-form. "Monks!
One then reflects and contemplates thus:"
"For what reason is there consciousness?
And by what causes and conditions is there further consciousness?
"Monks! [he said.]
Then, reflecting upon the original contemplation, he had this realization:
"Because of name-and-form there is consciousness; furthermore, name-and-form is also the causal condition for consciousness. "Monks!"
He then reflected and gave rise to this thought:
"What kind of thing is this consciousness that has returned and no longer remains as before?
Name-and-form conditions consciousness, and consciousness also conditions name-and-form."
Name-and-form has the six sense bases as its condition; the six sense bases have contact as their condition;
contact has feeling as its condition; feeling has craving as its condition;
craving has grasping as its condition; grasping has becoming as its condition.
With conditions there is birth; with birth as condition, there is old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress. From these, existence arises.
Thus, it is solely from the five aggregates that all suffering arises through accumulation.
"Monks! He then reflected to himself:
'For what reason is there no aging and death?'"
"And for what reason do aging and death cease?
Then, O bhikṣus, by reflecting according to his original mindfulness, he attained this realization that was agreeable to his mind:
"When there is no birth, there is neither aging nor death; with the exhaustion of birth, aging and death are also exhausted. "Monks!
He then reflects to himself:"
"Why is it that one is no longer reborn?
And by what causes and conditions is rebirth brought to an end?
"O Bhikṣus! [the Buddha replied.]
Then, reflecting upon the fundamental mindfulness, he gave rise to this appropriate thought:
"If that which exists were to exist [permanently], it would not arise again;
when existence is exhausted, its arising is likewise exhausted."
"Monks! He then reflects and contemplates:
'What is it that, being non-existent, is [regarded] as existent?'"
"What kind of exhaustion is there that leads to further exhaustion?
O monks, they then reflected according to their original mindfulness, and within themselves, a corresponding realization arose:
"When there is no grasping, there is non-existence;
when grasping has been exhausted, there is exhaustion. "O bhikṣus!"
He then reflected:
"What is it that, by not existing, causes one to experience non-existence?
And what is it that, by being exhausted, causes one to experience exhaustion?"
"O bhikṣus! Then, reflecting according to the original mindfulness, he attained a realization in accordance with his intention:
'There is no craving, nor is there any grasping.'"
"When craving has been exhausted, one experiences exhaustion. "Monks!
Then they reflect and contemplate:"
"By what does the craving for existence cease?
What, when exhausted, results in the exhaustion of that craving?
"O monks! [the Buddha replied.]
He then reflected according to the original teaching, and his mind arose accordingly:
"When feeling does not exist, craving does not exist;
with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases."
“O bhikṣus! They then reflected and considered:
‘What being absent would there be no feeling?’”
"What is the exhaustion that constitutes the exhaustion of feeling?
He then reflected upon his original mindfulness and attained this realization:
"When contact does not exist, then feeling does not exist."
"When contact ceases, feeling also ceases.
He then further reflected:
"What being absent causes contact to be absent?"
"What is it that, when exhausted, results in the exhaustion of contact?
He then reflected upon his former lives and attained a realization in accordance with his mind:
"When the six sense bases do not exist, then contact does not exist."
"When the six sense bases cease, contact ceases.
He then further reflected:
"What must be absent for the six sense bases to be absent?"
"What must be exhausted for the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) to be exhausted?
Then, reflecting upon his original mindfulness, he attained this realization:
"When name-and-form (nāmarūpa) does not exist, the six sense bases do not exist."
"When name-and-form (nāmarūpa) ceases, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) also cease. He then further reflected:
"In the absence of what do name-and-form cease?"
"What is meant by 'the exhaustion of what is exhausted,' and also the exhaustion of names and forms?
He then reflected again, following his original contemplation, and this thought arose:
"Where there is no consciousness, there are also no names and forms."
"When consciousness is exhausted, it is further called the exhaustion of name-and-form. He then reflected again:
"What must be absent for consciousness to be absent?"
"What is it that, when exhausted, causes consciousness to be exhausted?
He then reflected upon his original contemplation and attained this realization:
"When there is no seed of calamity, consciousness likewise does not exist."
"When the seeds of calamity are exhausted, then consciousness is exhausted.
He then further reflected and thought:
"What must be absent for the seeds of calamity to be absent?"
"What is it that, when exhausted, constitutes the exhaustion of the seeds of calamity?
He then reflected upon his origins and attained a realization in accordance with his mind:
"Where there is no delusion, there are also no seeds of calamity."
When delusion is exhausted, the seeds of calamity are exhausted;
when the seeds of calamity are exhausted, consciousness is exhausted;
when consciousness is exhausted, name-and-form are exhausted.
When name-and-form (nāmarūpa) ceases, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) cease;
when the six sense bases cease, contact (sparśa) ceases;
when contact ceases, sensation (vedanā) ceases.
With the exhaustion of sensation and perception, craving is exhausted;
with the exhaustion of craving, grasping is exhausted;
with the exhaustion of grasping, existence is exhausted.
With the exhaustion of existence, birth is exhausted;
with the exhaustion of birth, old age and death are exhausted, and sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress are likewise exhausted.
In this way, the immeasurable mass of suffering is brought to an end.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, he thought thus because he had attained the path himself.
The Buddha went from there, and he followed as soon as he obtained [the opportunity]."

Having followed [the path], one then knows old age and death, knows the origin of old age and death, knows the cessation of old age and death, and knows the practice for transcending old age and death.
It is the same for birth, for existence, for sensation, for craving, for feeling, for contact, for the six sense bases, for name-and-form, for consciousness, and for the constituent of becoming.
One thus knows delusion, and also knows the origin of delusion, and also knows where delusion ceases, and also knows the practice that leads to the cessation of delusion.
It is like this, bhikṣu:
suppose a person is traveling through a desolate wilderness in a secluded place and sees an ancient path, the traces of those who have traveled it in the past; the person then follows those traces.
Having followed the path, he saw an ancient city, a park with abundant trees, ponds, rivers, mountains, and moats; it was a place of great prosperity and delightful gardens.
He then thought to himself: "If I go now, I shall inform the King:

'While wandering in the empty wilderness at a secluded spot, I saw an ancient road and the traces of those who had walked before. Following them, I saw an ancient city, a park with abundant trees, ponds, rivers, mountains, and moats; it is a place of great prosperity and delightful gardens, fit for the King to dwell in.'"
The king then took up residence there.
After some time, it gradually became more secure and increasingly prosperous, becoming a place of great abundance and many people.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I am also like this: having found the ancient path upon which the Buddhas of old traveled, I followed it;

having followed it, I have come to know the origin of old age and death, I have known the accumulation of old age and death, I have known how old age and death are extinguished, and I have known the practice by which one transcends the world through old age and death."

Knowing birth is likewise; knowing existence is likewise; knowing sensation is likewise; knowing craving is likewise; knowing feeling is likewise; knowing contact is likewise; knowing the six sense bases is likewise; knowing name-and-form is likewise; knowing consciousness is likewise; knowing volitional formations is likewise;
one knows ignorance, and also knows from what ignorance arises, and also knows from what ignorance ceases, and also knows what practice removes ignorance and leads to transcendence in the world.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās:
“If a bhikṣu, for the sake of a bhikṣu, practices as he ought to practice, he shall attain the Way, not lose the Way, and be skillful in the Way.”
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs, it is the same for upāsakas, and it is the same for upāsikās.
If one truly receives and practices correctly, one will then follow the Path and attain the Path.
"One who is able to practice in accordance with the Dharma, such a practitioner of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), will increase and eventually arrive [at the goal].
Having seen the Buddha speak thus, both gods and humans took it to heart; those who practice as the Buddha taught received it.
The Sutra on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under the Pippala Tree.
